False

questions.solution_md: False. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of the **solvent**, not of the solution.

questions.stem_md: $4.0\ \text{g}$ of sodium hydroxide ($M = 40\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to $250\ \text{mL}$. Find its molarity in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Moles of NaOH $= \dfrac{4.0}{40} = 0.1$.

Step 2 — Volume $= 0.250\ \text{L}$, so molarity $= \dfrac{0.1}{0.250} = 0.4$, that is $0.4\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Divides by 0.250 L to get 0.4 M

questions.stem_md: A coolant is made by dissolving $6.2\ \text{g}$ of ethylene glycol ($\ce{C2H6O2}$) in $200\ \text{g}$ of water. Find the molality of the solution in $\text{mol kg}^{-1}$. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Molar mass of $\ce{C2H6O2}$ $= 2 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 + 2 \times 16 = 62$, in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Step 2 — Moles $= \dfrac{6.2}{62} = 0.1$.

Step 3 — Molality $= \dfrac{0.1}{0.200} = 0.5$, that is $0.5\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A sample of a hand-rub liquid is 46% ethanol ($\ce{C2H5OH}$) by mass in water. Find the mole fraction of ethanol in it.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take $100\ \text{g}$ of the liquid: $46\ \text{g}$ ethanol and $54\ \text{g}$ water.

Moles of ethanol $= \dfrac{46}{46} = 1$; moles of water $= \dfrac{54}{18} = 3$.

$x_\text{ethanol} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 3} = 0.25$.

questions.solution_md: Assume 100 g of liquid, convert each mass to moles, then divide the ethanol moles by the total.

marking_scheme.step: Moles of ethanol (1) and of water (3) from 100 g

questions.stem_md: Why is molality preferred to molarity for expressing concentration in experiments on boiling and freezing points?

answer.model_answer_md: Molarity uses the volume of the solution, and volume changes when a liquid is heated or cooled, so molarity changes with temperature. Molality uses the mass of the solvent, which does not change, so it stays constant over the temperature range of such experiments.

questions.solution_md: Contrast the volume basis of molarity with the mass basis of molality.

marking_scheme.step: Molarity depends on volume, which changes with temperature
Molality depends on mass, which does not

questions.stem_md: A fertiliser solution is $15\%$ urea ($\ce{NH2CONH2}$, $M = 60\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) by mass and has a density of $1.05\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$. Calculate (a) its molality, (b) its molarity and (c) the mole fraction of urea.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take $100\ \text{g}$ of solution: $15\ \text{g}$ urea $= \dfrac{15}{60} = 0.25\ \text{mol}$; water $= 85\ \text{g} \approx 4.72\ \text{mol}$.

(a) Molality $= \dfrac{0.25}{0.085} \approx 2.94\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

(b) Volume $= \dfrac{100}{1.05} \approx 95.2\ \text{mL}$; molarity $= \dfrac{0.25}{0.0952} \approx 2.63\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

(c) $x_\text{urea} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 + 4.72} \approx 0.050$.

questions.solution_md: Assume 100 g of solution; use the solvent mass for molality, density for the volume and total moles for the mole fraction.

questions.stem_md: Match each concentration term with its definition.

options.text_md: Molarity
Molality
Mole fraction
Parts per million

match_right.text_md: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Parts of a component per $10^{6}$ parts of solution
Moles of solute per litre of solution
Moles of a component divided by total moles

questions.solution_md: Molarity uses litres of solution, molality uses kilograms of solvent, mole fraction is a ratio of moles, and ppm compares parts with a million parts.

questions.stem_md: Henry’s law constants in water at the same temperature are: gas P $= 0.5\ \text{kbar}$, gas Q $= 30\ \text{kbar}$, gas R $= 75\ \text{kbar}$, gas S $= 145\ \text{kbar}$. At the same partial pressure, which gas is **least** soluble?

options.text_md: P
Q
R
S

questions.solution_md: From $p = K_\text{H}\,x$, $x = \dfrac{p}{K_\text{H}}$: at equal $p$ the largest $K_\text{H}$ gives the smallest mole fraction. S has the largest constant — option (d). P (a) is the most soluble.

questions.stem_md: On a hot afternoon, fish in a shallow pond swim near the surface and gulp air. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: the solubility of oxygen in water falls as the temperature rises
the solubility of oxygen in water rises as the temperature rises
warm water has a higher Henry’s law constant for oxygen, so it holds more oxygen
the partial pressure of oxygen in the air falls in the afternoon

questions.solution_md: Dissolving a gas releases heat, and $K_\text{H}$ increases with temperature, so warm water holds less oxygen — option (a). (b) reverses the trend; (c) wrongly links a higher $K_\text{H}$ to higher solubility; (d) is not true — the air’s oxygen content does not change.

questions.stem_md: Dissolving salt X in water absorbs heat, while dissolving salt Y releases heat. What happens to their solubilities when the temperature of the water is raised?

options.text_md: Both increase.
Solubility of X increases; solubility of Y decreases.
Solubility of X decreases; solubility of Y increases.
Neither changes, because pressure is constant.

questions.solution_md: By Le Chatelier’s principle, heating favours the direction that absorbs heat. For X dissolving absorbs heat, so more dissolves; for Y dissolving releases heat, so less dissolves — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why do the air tanks of deep-sea divers contain air diluted with helium?

options.text_md: Helium makes the air denser, so the diver sinks faster.
Helium is much less soluble in blood than nitrogen, so fewer bubbles form when the diver rises.
Helium reacts with nitrogen to remove it from the blood.
Helium is more soluble than nitrogen and dissolves instead of it.

questions.solution_md: Under high pressure, nitrogen dissolves in the blood and bubbles out on rapid ascent (the bends). Helium has a very large Henry’s constant, so little of it dissolves — option (b). Helium is unreactive (c), less dense (a) and less soluble, not more (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Aquatic animals are more comfortable in cold water than in warm water.

**Reason (R):** The Henry’s law constant of oxygen in water decreases as the temperature rises.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: cold water holds more dissolved oxygen. R is false: $K_\text{H}$ **increases** with temperature, which is why oxygen is less soluble in warm water — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The painful condition caused when nitrogen dissolved in a diver’s blood forms bubbles during a rapid ascent is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: Rapid fall in pressure lets dissolved nitrogen escape as bubbles in the blood: the **bends**.

questions.stem_md: What partial pressure of carbon dioxide, in **bar**, is needed above water at $298\ \text{K}$ for the mole fraction of dissolved $\ce{CO2}$ to be $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$? ($K_\text{H} = 1.67\ \text{kbar}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $K_\text{H} = 1.67\ \text{kbar} = 1670\ \text{bar}$.

Step 2 — $p = K_\text{H}\,x = 1670 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.67$, so the pressure is $1.67\ \text{bar}$.

marking_scheme.step: Converts kbar to bar and uses p = KH x

questions.stem_md: Use Henry’s law to explain (a) why a cold drink bottle fizzes when it is opened, and (b) why climbers at high altitude can feel weak and confused.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The drink is sealed under a high pressure of carbon dioxide, so much gas is dissolved. Opening the bottle lowers the pressure, the solubility falls and the extra gas escapes as bubbles. (b) At high altitude the partial pressure of oxygen is low, so less oxygen dissolves in the blood (anoxia).

questions.solution_md: Link each effect to a change in partial pressure, which changes the amount of gas dissolved.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Pressure falls on opening, so dissolved CO₂ comes out
(b) Low partial pressure of oxygen, less dissolves in blood

questions.stem_md: A student says, "Heating always increases the solubility of a solid in water." Is the student right? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Not always. If dissolving absorbs heat, raising the temperature increases solubility. If dissolving releases heat, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium back towards the solid, so solubility decreases. The effect depends on the enthalpy of solution, by Le Chatelier’s principle.

questions.solution_md: The direction depends on whether dissolving is endothermic or exothermic.

marking_scheme.step: States the claim is not always true
Endothermic: increases; exothermic: decreases, with Le Chatelier

questions.stem_md: Air at sea level has an oxygen partial pressure of $0.21\ \text{bar}$; at a hill station it is about $0.16\ \text{bar}$. $K_\text{H}$ for oxygen in water is $34.86\ \text{kbar}$ (take it as the same at both places). (a) Find the mole fraction of oxygen in water at sea level. (b) How many millimoles of oxygen dissolve in $1\ \text{L}$ ($1000\ \text{g}$) of water at sea level? (c) By what percentage is the dissolved oxygen lower at the hill station?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $x = \dfrac{p}{K_\text{H}} = \dfrac{0.21}{34860} \approx 6.02 \times 10^{-6}$.

(b) Moles of water $= \dfrac{1000}{18} \approx 55.6$; $n_{\ce{O2}} \approx 6.02 \times 10^{-6} \times 55.6 \approx 3.35 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol} \approx 0.335\ \text{mmol}$.

(c) Dissolved oxygen is proportional to $p$: fall $= \dfrac{0.21 - 0.16}{0.21} \times 100 \approx 23.8\%$ lower.

questions.solution_md: Use x = p/KH with p and KH in bar, multiply by the moles of water, then compare the two pressures.

questions.stem_md: Two liquids warm up when they are mixed, and the volume of the mixture is slightly less than the sum of their separate volumes. The solution:

options.text_md: shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law
is an ideal solution
must form a minimum-boiling azeotrope
shows negative deviation from Raoult’s law

questions.solution_md: Warming means $\Delta_\text{mix}H < 0$ and contraction means $\Delta_\text{mix}V < 0$: new A–B attractions are stronger, molecules escape less easily and the vapour pressure is lower than predicted — option (d). An ideal solution (b) has no heat or volume change; a minimum-boiling azeotrope (c) comes from positive deviation (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of liquids forms a solution that is very nearly ideal?

options.text_md: Chloroform and acetone
Ethanol and acetone
n-Hexane and n-heptane
Nitric acid and water

questions.solution_md: n-Hexane and n-heptane are similar non-polar molecules, so A–B attractions match A–A and B–B attractions — option (c). Chloroform–acetone (a) and nitric acid–water (d) show negative deviation; ethanol–acetone (b) shows positive deviation.

questions.stem_md: An ideal solution of liquids A and B is in equilibrium with its vapour. Pure A is more volatile than pure B. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The mole fraction of A is larger in the vapour than in the liquid.
The vapour and the liquid have the same composition.
The mole fraction of A is smaller in the vapour than in the liquid.
The vapour contains only A.

questions.solution_md: $y_\text{A} = \dfrac{p^\circ_\text{A} x_\text{A}}{p_\text{total}}$, and $p^\circ_\text{A}$ is greater than $p_\text{total}$ because A is the more volatile component, so $y_\text{A} > x_\text{A}$ — option (a). Equal compositions (b) occur only at an azeotrope, which an ideal solution never forms.

questions.stem_md: Rectified spirit (about 95% ethanol) cannot be turned into pure ethanol by fractional distillation because:

options.text_md: it is a maximum-boiling azeotrope caused by negative deviation
ethanol and water have the same boiling point
ethanol and water form an ideal solution
it is a minimum-boiling azeotrope, whose vapour has the same composition as the liquid

questions.solution_md: Ethanol and water show large positive deviation and form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95% ethanol; at that composition the vapour matches the liquid, so distillation cannot separate them — option (d). The boiling points differ (b), the solution is not ideal (c), and the deviation is positive (a).

questions.stem_md: Liquids A ($p^\circ = 24\ \text{kPa}$) and B ($p^\circ = 56\ \text{kPa}$) form an ideal solution. For an equimolar liquid mixture, the mole fraction of B in the vapour is:
questions.solution_md: $p_\text{A} = 24 \times 0.5 = 12$, $p_\text{B} = 56 \times 0.5 = 28$, total $40\ \text{kPa}$. $y_\text{B} = \dfrac{28}{40} = 0.70$ — option (c). (a) is the liquid composition; (b) is $y_\text{A}$; (d) copies the vapour pressure of B.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mixture of chloroform and acetone shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

**Reason (R):** Chloroform molecules form hydrogen bonds with acetone molecules.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: the C–H of chloroform hydrogen-bonds to the oxygen of acetone. These new attractions are stronger, so the mixture shows **negative** deviation; A is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law in which the Henry’s law constant equals the vapour pressure of the pure component.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Both laws have the form $p = (\text{constant}) \times x$; in Raoult’s law the constant is $p^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A solution showing large negative deviation from Raoult’s law forms a ___-boiling azeotrope.
questions.solution_md: Negative deviation lowers the vapour pressure, so the mixture boils at a temperature above both components: a **maximum**-boiling azeotrope.

questions.stem_md: Match each mixture with its behaviour.

options.text_md: n-Hexane + n-heptane
Ethanol + acetone
Chloroform + acetone
Nitric acid (about 68%) + water

questions.solution_md: Similar alkanes are nearly ideal; acetone breaks the hydrogen bonds of ethanol (positive); chloroform hydrogen-bonds to acetone (negative); nitric acid and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

questions.stem_md: $2\ \text{mol}$ of liquid A ($p^\circ = 40\ \text{kPa}$) is mixed with $3\ \text{mol}$ of liquid B ($p^\circ = 90\ \text{kPa}$) to form an ideal solution. Find the total vapour pressure in **kPa**.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $x_\text{A} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$, $x_\text{B} = 0.6$.

Step 2 — $p_\text{A} = 40 \times 0.4 = 16$; $p_\text{B} = 90 \times 0.6 = 54$.

Step 3 — Total $= 16 + 54 = 70$, so $70\ \text{kPa}$.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between an ideal solution and a non-ideal solution showing positive deviation.

answer.model_answer_md: An ideal solution obeys Raoult’s law at every composition, while a positive-deviation solution has a vapour pressure higher than predicted. For an ideal solution $\Delta_\text{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_\text{mix}V = 0$; for positive deviation both are positive, because A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B.

questions.solution_md: Compare obedience to Raoult’s law and the signs of the enthalpy and volume of mixing.

marking_scheme.step: Difference 1: Raoult’s law obeyed vs vapour pressure higher
Difference 2: ΔmixH and ΔmixV zero vs positive (weaker A–B forces)

questions.stem_md: Explain, in terms of intermolecular attractions, why (a) a mixture of ethanol and acetone shows positive deviation, and (b) a mixture of chloroform and acetone shows negative deviation. (c) State the sign of the enthalpy of mixing in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Pure ethanol is held together by hydrogen bonds. Acetone molecules come between ethanol molecules and break some of these bonds, and the new ethanol–acetone attractions are weaker, so molecules escape more easily and the vapour pressure is higher than predicted. (b) Chloroform’s hydrogen forms a hydrogen bond with acetone’s oxygen; these new attractions are stronger, so molecules escape less easily. (c) Ethanol + acetone: positive (heat absorbed); chloroform + acetone: negative (heat released).

questions.solution_md: Weaker A–B attraction means positive deviation and endothermic mixing; stronger means negative deviation and exothermic mixing.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Acetone breaks ethanol’s hydrogen bonds, weaker A–B attractions
(b) New hydrogen bonds between chloroform and acetone, stronger attractions
(c) Positive for ethanol + acetone; negative for chloroform + acetone

questions.stem_md: Which of these is **not** a colligative property?

options.text_md: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
Vapour pressure of the solution
Depression of freezing point
Osmotic pressure

questions.solution_md: The vapour pressure of a solution depends on the nature of the solvent as well, so it is not colligative; the **relative lowering** of vapour pressure depends only on the solute’s mole fraction — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which $0.1\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ aqueous solution has the **lowest** freezing point? (Assume complete dissociation of salts.)

options.text_md: Potassium sulfate
Glucose
Sodium chloride
Urea

questions.solution_md: Depression is proportional to the number of particles, $i\,m$. Glucose and urea give 1 particle ($i = 1$), sodium chloride 2, and potassium sulfate $\ce{K2SO4 -> 2K+ + SO4^2-}$ gives 3, so it shows the largest depression and the lowest freezing point — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A red blood cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What happens?

options.text_md: Water enters the cell and it swells and bursts.
Salt enters the cell and it shrinks.
Water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks.
Nothing happens, because the cell membrane is semipermeable.

questions.solution_md: The salt solution is hypertonic: water moves from the cell (more dilute inside) to the outside — option (c). Swelling (a) happens in a hypotonic solution such as pure water; salt does not cross the membrane (b); a semipermeable membrane is exactly what allows osmosis (d).

questions.stem_md: The molar mass of a newly isolated enzyme is best found by measuring:

options.text_md: the elevation of boiling point of its aqueous solution
the depression of freezing point of its solution in benzene
the osmotic pressure of its dilute solution at room temperature
the relative lowering of vapour pressure of its solution

questions.solution_md: Enzymes are damaged by heat, and their huge molar masses give tiny boiling or freezing point changes and vapour pressure lowering. Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature and is large enough to read even for very dilute solutions — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The SI-based unit of the ebullioscopic constant $K_\text{b}$ is:

options.text_md: $\text{K mol kg}^{-1}$
$\text{mol kg K}^{-1}$
$\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$
$\text{K L mol}^{-1}$

questions.solution_md: From $\Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b}\,m$, $K_\text{b} = \dfrac{\Delta T_\text{b}}{m}$ has unit $\dfrac{\text{K}}{\text{mol kg}^{-1}} = \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A $0.1\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ sodium chloride solution boils at a higher temperature than a $0.1\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ glucose solution.

**Reason (R):** The elevation of boiling point depends on the chemical nature of the solute.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: sodium chloride gives about twice as many particles. R is false: colligative properties depend on the **number** of particles, not on their nature — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A 0.9% (mass by volume) sodium chloride solution is isotonic with the fluid inside red blood cells.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. This is why “normal saline” drips use about 0.9% sodium chloride; the cells neither shrink nor swell.

questions.stem_md: The depression of freezing point for a solution of molality one mole per kilogram is called the ___ constant.
questions.solution_md: $K_\text{f}$ is the **cryoscopic** (molal depression) constant.

questions.stem_md: A membrane that allows solvent molecules but not solute particles to pass through is called a ___ membrane.
questions.solution_md: Such a membrane is **semipermeable**; osmosis takes place through it.

questions.stem_md: $3.0\ \text{g}$ of urea ($M = 60\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) is dissolved in $250\ \text{g}$ of water. Find the elevation of boiling point in **kelvin**. ($K_\text{b} = 0.52\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Molality $= \dfrac{3.0/60}{0.250} = 0.2$, in $\text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

Step 2 — $\Delta T_\text{b} = 0.52 \times 0.2 = 0.104$, so the elevation is $0.104\ \text{K}$.

questions.stem_md: $2.5\ \text{g}$ of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute dissolved in $100\ \text{g}$ of benzene lowers its freezing point by $0.512\ \text{K}$. Find the molar mass of the solute in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$. ($K_\text{f}$ of benzene $= 5.12\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $M_2 = \dfrac{K_\text{f} \times 1000 \times w_2}{\Delta T_\text{f} \times w_1}$.

Step 2 — $M_2 = \dfrac{5.12 \times 1000 \times 2.5}{0.512 \times 100} = 250$, so the molar mass is $250\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A glucose solution contains $0.02\ \text{mol}$ of glucose per litre. Find its osmotic pressure in **bar** at $300\ \text{K}$. ($R = 0.083\ \text{L bar K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\pi = CRT = 0.02 \times 0.083 \times 300 = 0.498$, so the osmotic pressure is $0.498\ \text{bar}$.

marking_scheme.step: π = CRT with C = 0.02, T = 300 K, π = 0.498 bar

questions.stem_md: Define the molal elevation constant and explain why a solution of a non-volatile solute boils at a higher temperature than the pure solvent.

answer.model_answer_md: The molal elevation (ebullioscopic) constant is the elevation of boiling point for a solution of molality one mole per kilogram. The solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent, so the solution must be heated to a higher temperature before its vapour pressure equals the atmospheric pressure.

questions.solution_md: Define Kb, then link the lower vapour pressure to a higher boiling point.

marking_scheme.step: Lower vapour pressure, reaches atmospheric pressure at a higher temperature

questions.stem_md: Explain why (a) raw mango slices placed in thick salt solution shrivel, and (b) wilted flowers revive when their stems are placed in fresh water.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The salt solution is hypertonic to the mango cells, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis and the slices shrink and shrivel. (b) Fresh water is hypotonic to the cells of the stem and petals, so water enters them by osmosis, the cells become firm again and the flowers revive.

questions.solution_md: Water moves by osmosis from the more dilute side into the more concentrated side.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Hypertonic outside, water leaves the cells
(b) Hypotonic outside, water enters the cells

questions.stem_md: At a certain temperature, the vapour pressure of pure water is $3.200\ \text{kPa}$. When $10\ \text{g}$ of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in $200\ \text{g}$ of water, the vapour pressure falls to $3.184\ \text{kPa}$. Using the dilute-solution approximation, find the molar mass of the solute.

answer.model_answer_md:
Relative lowering $= \dfrac{3.200 - 3.184}{3.200} = 0.005$.

For a dilute solution $\dfrac{\Delta p}{p^\circ} \approx \dfrac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1}$, so $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2 M_1}{w_1 \times 0.005}$.

$M_2 = \dfrac{10 \times 18}{200 \times 0.005} = 180$, so the molar mass is about $180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute; use the dilute form with masses and molar masses.

questions.stem_md: Normal saline contains $9.0\ \text{g}$ of sodium chloride ($M = 58.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) per litre. Assuming complete dissociation, (a) find the total molar concentration of particles, (b) find the mass of glucose ($M = 180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) per litre that would give an isotonic solution at the same temperature, and (c) explain why the factor for sodium chloride is taken as 2.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{9.0}{58.5} \approx 0.154\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ of NaCl; with $i = 2$, particles $\approx 0.308\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

(b) Isotonic solutions have equal $\pi$, so glucose ($i = 1$) must be $0.308\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$: mass $\approx 0.308 \times 180 \approx 55.4\ \text{g}$ per litre (about 5.5% w/v).

(c) Each formula unit gives two ions, $\ce{NaCl -> Na+ + Cl-}$, and osmotic pressure counts particles.

questions.solution_md: Equal osmotic pressure means equal concentration of particles, i × C.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Two ions per formula unit; colligative properties count particles

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The van’t Hoff factor for ethanoic acid dissolved in benzene is less than 1.

**Reason (R):** In benzene, ethanoic acid molecules pair up into dimers through hydrogen bonding.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Dimerisation reduces the number of particles, so the observed colligative effect is smaller than calculated and $i < 1$; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Assuming complete dissociation, the van’t Hoff factor of potassium sulfate in water is:
questions.solution_md: $\ce{K2SO4 -> 2K+ + SO4^2-}$ gives three ions per formula unit, so $i = 3$ — option (d). (a) counts kinds of ion, (b) counts atoms, and (c) ignores dissociation.

questions.stem_md: The molar mass of potassium chloride ($74.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) found from the freezing point of its dilute aqueous solution is close to $40\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. This is because:

options.text_md: potassium chloride dissociates into ions, increasing the number of particles
potassium chloride associates into pairs, decreasing the number of particles
potassium chloride is volatile and escapes from the solution
the freezing point method always gives half the true molar mass

questions.solution_md: More particles give a larger depression, which the formula reads as a smaller molar mass: $i \approx \dfrac{74.5}{40} \approx 1.86$, consistent with nearly complete dissociation into two ions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In benzene, the molar mass of a carboxylic acid found from the depression of freezing point is almost exactly twice the value from its formula. The van’t Hoff factor and the best explanation are:

options.text_md: 2; the acid dissociates into two ions in benzene
0.5; the acid dissociates into two ions in benzene
2; the acid is almost completely dimerised
0.5; the acid is almost completely dimerised through hydrogen bonds

questions.solution_md: $i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$. questions.stem_md:
(a) State Raoult’s law for a solution of two volatile liquids and derive an expression for the total vapour pressure in terms of the mole fraction of one component.

(b) Sketch the graph of partial and total vapour pressures against composition for an ideal solution.

(c) Liquids X ($p^\circ = 80\ \text{kPa}$) and Y ($p^\circ = 20\ \text{kPa}$) form an ideal solution in which $x_\text{X} = 0.3$. Find the total vapour pressure and the mole fraction of X in the vapour. Comment on your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: $p_1 = p^\circ_1 x_1$, $p_2 = p^\circ_2 x_2$. By Dalton’s law, $p_\text{total} = p^\circ_1 x_1 + p^\circ_2 x_2$; with $x_1 = 1 - x_2$, $p_\text{total} = p^\circ_1 + (p^\circ_2 - p^\circ_1)x_2$.

(b) Mole fraction on the x-axis, vapour pressure on the y-axis: $p_1$ is a straight line falling from $p^\circ_1$ to 0, $p_2$ a straight line rising from 0 to $p^\circ_2$, and $p_\text{total}$ a straight line joining $p^\circ_1$ and $p^\circ_2$.

(c) $p_\text{X} = 80 \times 0.3 = 24\ \text{kPa}$; $p_\text{Y} = 20 \times 0.7 = 14\ \text{kPa}$; total $= 38\ \text{kPa}$. $y_\text{X} = \dfrac{24}{38} \approx 0.63$. The vapour is much richer in X (0.63) than the liquid (0.3), because X is the more volatile liquid.

questions.solution_md: Raoult + Dalton gives the straight-line total pressure; the more volatile component is enriched in the vapour.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Derivation of the total pressure expression
(b) Correctly labelled graph with three straight lines

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are non-ideal solutions? Explain positive and negative deviations from Raoult’s law with one example of each, giving the signs of the enthalpy and volume of mixing.

(b) Draw a graph of total vapour pressure against composition for each type of deviation.

(c) What is an azeotrope? Which type of azeotrope does each deviation produce?

answer.model_answer_md: Non-ideal solutions do not obey Raoult’s law over the whole range of composition. In **positive** deviation, A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B, so the vapour pressure is higher than predicted, mixing absorbs heat and the volume increases; example: ethanol and acetone. In **negative** deviation, A–B attractions are stronger, vapour pressure is lower, mixing releases heat and the volume decreases; example: chloroform and acetone, which hydrogen-bond. On the graph, positive deviation curves above the straight Raoult line and negative deviation below it. An azeotrope boils at constant temperature with identical liquid and vapour composition. Positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope; negative gives a maximum-boiling one.

questions.solution_md: Link the strength of A–B attractions to vapour pressure, heat and volume; then link the deviation type to the azeotrope type.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Two correct graphs relative to the Raoult line

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are colligative properties? Name the four colligative properties.

(b) Explain, with reference to vapour pressure, why the freezing point of a solvent is lowered when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it.

(c) $1.0\ \text{g}$ of a sample of sulfur dissolved in $50\ \text{g}$ of benzene lowers the freezing point of benzene by $0.40\ \text{K}$. Find the molar mass of sulfur in this solution and the number of atoms in each sulfur molecule. ($K_\text{f}$ of benzene $= 5.12\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$; S = 32)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles in a given amount of solvent, not on their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.

(b) At the freezing point, the liquid solvent and solid solvent have the same vapour pressure. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid, so the two vapour pressures become equal only at a lower temperature; the solution therefore freezes below the pure solvent ($\Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f}\,m$).

(c) $M_2 = \dfrac{K_\text{f} \times 1000 \times w_2}{\Delta T_\text{f} \times w_1} = \dfrac{5.12 \times 1000 \times 1.0}{0.40 \times 50} = 256$, in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$. Atoms per molecule $= \dfrac{256}{32} = 8$, so sulfur is present as $\ce{S8}$.

questions.solution_md: Define, explain through equal vapour pressures of solid and liquid, then use the molar-mass form of ΔTf = Kf m.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Vapour pressure explanation of freezing point depression

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define osmosis and osmotic pressure.

(b) Show that the molar mass of a solute can be found from $\pi = CRT$, and give two reasons why this method is preferred for polymers.

(c) $1.5\ \text{g}$ of a polymer is dissolved to make $500\ \text{mL}$ of solution at $27\ ^\circ\text{C}$. The osmotic pressure is $6.225 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{bar}$. Find the molar mass of the polymer. ($R = 0.083\ \text{L bar K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Osmosis is the net flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent (or a dilute solution) into a more concentrated solution. Osmotic pressure is the excess pressure that must be applied to the solution to just stop this flow.

(b) $\pi = CRT = \dfrac{n_2}{V}RT = \dfrac{w_2 RT}{M_2 V}$, so $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2 RT}{\pi V}$. Preferred for polymers because it is measured at room temperature (no heat damage), and because it gives large, measurable values even for very dilute solutions of high molar mass solutes.

(c) $T = 300\ \text{K}$, $V = 0.500\ \text{L}$. $M_2 = \dfrac{1.5 \times 0.083 \times 300}{6.225 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.500} = \dfrac{37.35}{3.1125 \times 10^{-4}} = 120000$, so the molar mass is $1.2 \times 10^{5}\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Rearrange π = CRT with n = w/M; use V in litres and T in kelvin.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Substitution with T = 300 K, V = 0.5 L

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the van’t Hoff factor. Predict its value (greater than, less than or equal to 1) for (i) urea in water, (ii) sodium sulfate in water, (iii) benzoic acid in benzene.

(b) Write the expressions for $i$ in terms of the degree of dissociation (for a solute giving $n$ ions) and the degree of association (for dimers).

(c) $2.44\ \text{g}$ of benzoic acid ($M = 122\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) in $100\ \text{g}$ of benzene lowers the freezing point by $0.614\ \text{K}$. Find $i$ and the percentage of benzoic acid that is dimerised. ($K_\text{f}$ of benzene $= 5.12\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $i$ is the ratio of the observed colligative property to the value calculated assuming no dissociation or association (equivalently, normal molar mass ÷ abnormal molar mass). (i) Urea: $i = 1$; (ii) sodium sulfate: $i > 1$ (up to 3); (iii) benzoic acid in benzene: $i < 1$.

(b) Dissociation: $i = 1 + (n - 1)\alpha$. Dimerisation: $i = 1 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$.

(c) Normal molality $= \dfrac{2.44/122}{0.100} = 0.2\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$; calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 5.12 \times 0.2 = 1.024\ \text{K}$. $i = \dfrac{0.614}{1.024} \approx 0.60$. $\alpha = 2(1 - 0.60) = 0.80$, so about $80\%$ of the acid is dimerised.

questions.solution_md: Compare observed with calculated depression; for dimers α = 2(1 − i).
